variants.title: Follow one change to a decision
variants.context: An event-driven path detects a meaningful change, routes the timestamped event to connected cores, updates local neuron state until a threshold is crossed, then decodes a bounded decision. The user-visible metric belongs to that whole path.
variants.prompt: An event camera watches a conveyor for a dropped part. Put the stages in order for one meaningful change.

items.text: Decide: a readout converts spike timing, count, or state into the alert the operator sees.
Sense: the event sensor emits a timestamped change once its threshold is crossed.
Integrate: a neuron updates membrane state from the arrived event, leaks over time, and may fire.
Communicate: the event address and payload travel to the connected neuron cores.

variants.hint: Which stage owns the metric the user actually experiences?
variants.explanation: Efficiency claims belong to the complete sensor-to-decision path, because every boundary can add work the accelerator never sees.

variants.title: Follow one change to a decision
variants.context: An event-driven path detects a meaningful change, routes the timestamped event to connected cores, updates local neuron state until a threshold is crossed, then decodes a bounded decision. The user-visible metric belongs to that whole path.
variants.prompt: Someone lowers the sensor threshold to catch fainter parts, and traffic climbs. Put the stages in order, showing where the cost lands.

items.text: Integrate: neurons receive far more arrivals, so synaptic work follows the inflated event stream.
Sense: the lowered threshold emits many more timestamped changes, including noise.
Decide: the readout still must produce a decision inside its window despite the extra traffic.
Communicate: fan-out multiplies those events into routing pressure and deeper queues.

variants.hint: The threshold is one knob, but the cost appears at every later stage.
variants.explanation: A threshold too sensitive produces noise traffic, and sparse input is only useful when the whole path stays sparse.

variants.title: Follow one change to a decision
variants.context: An event-driven path detects a meaningful change, routes the timestamped event to connected cores, updates local neuron state until a threshold is crossed, then decodes a bounded decision. The user-visible metric belongs to that whole path.
variants.prompt: A dense tensor is rate-coded into spikes ahead of the network. Put the stages in order for that design.

items.text: Integrate: neurons accumulate over a long window before any threshold crossing is meaningful.
Communicate: the dense firing pattern occupies routes that a change-driven stream would leave idle.
Sense: an encoder turns a fixed-rate dense frame into a long rate-coded spike train.
Decide: the readout waits for the rate window to close, which extends time to first decision.

variants.hint: Ask what happened to sparsity at the very first boundary.
variants.explanation: Dense encoding erases the sparsity the hardware exploits, so conversion can preserve quality while removing the reason to use the device.

variants.title: Count the work honestly
variants.context: Three quantities stay separate: sensor event rate, synaptic additions equal to events times fan-out times layer activity, and dense update opportunities equal to fixed-rate samples times channels times possible connections in the matched baseline.
variants.prompt: An event sensor emits 20,000 events per second into a layer with fan-out 32, and only 50 percent of that layer is active. How many synaptic additions per second does the event path perform?
variants.hint: Fan-out and activity both scale the arriving events.
variants.explanation: Event-triggered synaptic work is input events times actual fan-out times layer activity, so idle regions of the network cost nothing.

mistakes.feedback: That applies the fan-out but ignores that only half the layer is active.
That applies the activity fraction but forgets each event reaches 32 connections.

variants.title: Count the work honestly
variants.context: Three quantities stay separate: sensor event rate, synaptic additions equal to events times fan-out times layer activity, and dense update opportunities equal to fixed-rate samples times channels times possible connections in the matched baseline.
variants.prompt: The matched dense baseline evaluates 2,000 samples per second across 64 channels with fan-out 16. How many dense synaptic opportunities does it count per second?
variants.hint: The dense side has no activity discount to apply.
variants.explanation: Dense opportunities are fixed-rate samples times channels times possible connections, which is the count an event path has to beat.

mistakes.feedback: That multiplies samples by channels and drops the fan-out of 16.
That multiplies samples by fan-out and drops the 64 channels.

variants.title: Count the work honestly
variants.context: Three quantities stay separate: sensor event rate, synaptic additions equal to events times fan-out times layer activity, and dense update opportunities equal to fixed-rate samples times channels times possible connections in the matched baseline.
variants.prompt: The dense baseline counts 1,600,000 synaptic opportunities per second while the event path performs 400,000 synaptic additions per second. The event path performs what percent of the dense work?
variants.hint: Put the event work over the dense work before scaling.
variants.explanation: Reporting event work as a share of the matched dense count is what turns two operation counts into a comparison a reader can check.

mistakes.feedback: That is the ratio of dense work to event work, not a percentage.
That divides dense by event work and then scales, which inverts the comparison.

variants.title: Complete the deployment contract
variants.context: A trained SNN is not a deployable system. The event contract defines inputs and overflow, the neuron contract defines dynamics and precision, the mapping contract partitions across cores, and the readout contract defines the decision window and fallback.
variants.prompt: A trained SNN is handed to the compiler team. Match each contract to what it must define.

pairs.label: Event contract
pairs.detail: Address, timestamp, polarity or payload, ordering, clock assumptions, and ingress overflow behavior.

pairs.label: Neuron contract
pairs.detail: State variables, integration, leak, threshold, reset, refractory behavior, precision, and learning rules.

pairs.label: Mapping contract
pairs.detail: Partitioning of neurons and synapses across cores under memory, fan-in, fan-out, routing, and delay limits.

pairs.label: Readout contract
pairs.detail: Decision window, decode rule, confidence, deadline, and fallback when events or timing become unreliable.

variants.hint: Each contract owns one translation that can silently change behavior.
variants.explanation: Every translation from training artifact to device can alter timing, precision, activity, or observability, so each one is specified and versioned.

variants.title: Complete the deployment contract
variants.context: A trained SNN is not a deployable system. The event contract defines inputs and overflow, the neuron contract defines dynamics and precision, the mapping contract partitions across cores, and the readout contract defines the decision window and fallback.
variants.prompt: Four findings appear during the mapping audit. Match each finding to the contract it belongs to.

pairs.label: The target cannot represent the trained refractory behavior
pairs.detail: The neuron contract, which must reject silent approximation.

pairs.label: One inter-core route saturates during bursts although its average is low
pairs.detail: The mapping contract, which bounds routing and placement.

pairs.label: The ingress queue has no defined behavior when it overflows
pairs.detail: The event contract, which must state overflow handling.

pairs.label: No rule exists for weak spike evidence at the deadline
pairs.detail: The readout contract, which defines confidence and fallback.

variants.hint: Sort by which translation the finding threatens.
variants.explanation: Audits check each contract separately, because an unrepresentable neuron and a saturating route are different failures with different owners.

variants.title: Complete the deployment contract
variants.context: A trained SNN is not a deployable system. The event contract defines inputs and overflow, the neuron contract defines dynamics and precision, the mapping contract partitions across cores, and the readout contract defines the decision window and fallback.
variants.prompt: The team lists the artifacts it will version alongside the model. Match each artifact to the contract it pins.

pairs.label: Sensor configuration and event schema
pairs.detail: The event contract, so inputs are reproducible across releases.

pairs.label: Quantization settings and neuron-model parameters
pairs.detail: The neuron contract, so dynamics match what was validated.

pairs.label: Compiler, mapper, and routing-table versions
pairs.detail: The mapping contract, so placement can be reproduced and compared.

pairs.label: Decision window and abstention policy
pairs.detail: The readout contract, so decisions stay comparable across runs.

variants.hint: Requalification is triggered by whichever pinned artifact changed.
variants.explanation: Versioning the whole path is what makes simulator-to-hardware regression tests meaningful after a compiler, firmware, or sensor change.

variants.title: Build a matched comparison
variants.context: A fair comparison fixes the task and quality target first, then measures every stage that produces the decision. Peak operations per watt characterizes hardware, not an application, so the boundary and the excluded costs are stated explicitly.
variants.prompt: A team wants to claim its event-driven path beats the dense baseline. Put the comparison steps in order.

items.text: Repeat across seeds, devices, environmental regimes, and warm and cold starts.
Freeze the event traces, task metric, quality floor, deadline, and confidence interval.
State which costs were measured, estimated, excluded, or amortized.
Tune a credible conventional baseline at the same boundary rather than a deliberately weak model.
Measure preprocessing through readout with synchronized energy and latency instrumentation.
Publish event rates, spike sparsity, operation counts, mapping utilization, and dropped-event behavior.

variants.hint: The claim is only as strong as the baseline it beat.
variants.explanation: Fixing the task and quality target first is what makes the later energy and latency numbers comparable at all.

variants.title: Build a matched comparison
variants.context: A fair comparison fixes the task and quality target first, then measures every stage that produces the decision. Peak operations per watt characterizes hardware, not an application, so the boundary and the excluded costs are stated explicitly.
variants.prompt: A vendor result cites energy per spike and peak synaptic operations per watt. Put the steps in order for turning that into an application claim.

items.text: Tune the conventional baseline to that same quality floor before any comparison is made.
Publish the workload metrics next to the system measurements without merging them into one number.
State clearly which costs were excluded or amortized in the reported figure.
Freeze the task, the quality floor, and the deadline the application actually requires.
Measure sensor, interfaces, host, accelerator, memory, and output over one wall-clock interval.

variants.hint: A hardware characterization is not yet an application result.
variants.explanation: Solution-level workload metrics and hardware-dependent system measurements stay linked but separate, since neither one substitutes for the other.

variants.title: Build a matched comparison
variants.context: A fair comparison fixes the task and quality target first, then measures every stage that produces the decision. Peak operations per watt characterizes hardware, not an application, so the boundary and the excluded costs are stated explicitly.
variants.prompt: A hybrid design sends ambiguous cases to a dense model. Put the comparison steps in order for that system.

items.text: Measure the event front end, the conversion, the dense fallback, and the readout as one path.
Freeze the task, quality floor, and deadline that apply to the combined system.
Tune the dense-only baseline at the same boundary so the hybrid is not compared to a weak model.
State which of those costs were measured and which were estimated or amortized.
Publish how often the fallback ran, along with sparsity and utilization for the event stage.

variants.hint: Whatever the fallback costs belongs inside the boundary.
variants.explanation: Conversion and fallback work counts in the measured boundary, otherwise the reported efficiency describes only the easy cases.

variants.title: Choose the training path
variants.context: Spikes are discrete, so training paths place the difficulty differently: surrogate gradients train the SNN directly, conversion starts from a dense model, local plasticity learns near the sensor, and hybrid designs must measure every conversion and fallback.
variants.prompt: An event-camera gesture system must produce a decision within 20 milliseconds and keep the input stream sparse. Which training path fits best?
options: Train the SNN with surrogate gradients against the exact target neuron model and sequence length.
Rely on local plasticity alone so the network learns the gestures directly from spike traces.
Convert a trained dense model into spike rates and lengthen the rate window until quality matches.
optionFeedback: Correct: surrogate gradients keep discrete spikes in the forward pass while training against the deployed neuron model and window.
Local plasticity adapts near the sensor but is a weak way to hit a specified task quality inside a fixed deadline.
A long rate window buys quality with latency and dense firing, which is exactly what the deadline and sparsity goal cannot afford.
variants.hint: Which option changes the latency and sparsity you were trying to protect?
variants.explanation: The training path is chosen by the deployment boundary, since each approach moves the discrete-spike difficulty to a different part of the system.

variants.title: Choose the training path
variants.context: Spikes are discrete, so training paths place the difficulty differently: surrogate gradients train the SNN directly, conversion starts from a dense model, local plasticity learns near the sensor, and hybrid designs must measure every conversion and fallback.
variants.prompt: A team wants on-device adaptation near the sensor using local plasticity after release. What must be true before that ships?
options: Updates are bounded by weight, rate, and time, with a rollbackable base configuration kept.
Adaptation is limited to the readout layer so the neuron dynamics can never be altered.
The plasticity rule is disabled whenever the device is running on battery power.
optionFeedback: Correct: online plasticity changes behavior after release, so bounded updates plus a base configuration to roll back to are the requirement.
Restricting the layer narrows the blast radius but still leaves unbounded drift within that layer.
Power state is unrelated to whether learned drift stays inside a validated envelope.
variants.hint: What happens to the validated behavior once weights keep moving in the field?
variants.explanation: Local plasticity is bounded by weight, rate, time, and rollback policy, because a released system that keeps learning can leave its evidence behind.

variants.title: Choose the training path
variants.context: Spikes are discrete, so training paths place the difficulty differently: surrogate gradients train the SNN directly, conversion starts from a dense model, local plasticity learns near the sensor, and hybrid designs must measure every conversion and fallback.
variants.prompt: A hybrid design uses an event front end and hands ambiguous cases to a dense model. What does the measured boundary have to include?
options: The event front end plus the accelerator time of the dense model when it is invoked.
Every stage including encoding, conversion, host transfers, the fallback, and the readout.
Only the event front end, since the dense model runs on separate hardware with its own budget.
optionFeedback: Counting only accelerator time omits encoding, host transfers, and readout, which is where hybrid designs often spend the difference.
Correct: the boundary covers preprocessing through readout, including retries and fallback, or the comparison is not matched.
Excluding the fallback reports the cost of the easy cases and calls it the system result.
variants.hint: Which work would a user still be paying for that this boundary might omit?
variants.explanation: Work evidence counts preprocessing, encoding, host transfers, routing, state updates, readout, retries, and fallback, not accelerator activity alone.
